A contestant is a person who enters and actively takes part in a competition — a contest where there is something to win, a result to be decided, or a title to be earned. The key idea is that this person is competing, meaning they are trying to outperform others, or at minimum, trying to achieve something that is being judged or measured against a standard.

Think of a game show on television. Several people sit under bright lights, answer questions, and try to win a cash prize. Each one of those people is a contestant.

Three things are almost always true about a contestant:

1. There is a contest or competition.
A contestant doesn't exist without a contest. You can't call someone a contestant if there is nothing to compete in. A contest can be a quiz, a race, a talent show, a sports event, a cooking competition — anything where performance is evaluated and a winner (or ranking) is determined.

2. They have voluntarily entered.
A contestant is not forced to be there. They have chosen to participate, usually by signing up, registering, or being selected to join. This sense of deliberate entry is built into the word.

3. They are active participants, not observers.
A person watching a competition from the crowd is an audience member or a spectator — not a contestant. A contestant is in the game, not watching it.
The Range of Situations Where This Word Is Used

The word "contestant" is used very broadly. Here are clear examples across different settings so you can see how flexible it is:

  • Game shows: "There were five contestants on the show, but only one walked away with the grand prize."
  • Beauty pageants: "She was a contestant in the national pageant and finished in second place."
  • Cooking competitions: "Each contestant had 30 minutes to prepare their dish for the judges."
  • Sports events (especially individual ones like wrestling or boxing): "The two contestants entered the ring to loud applause."
  • Talent shows: "The youngest contestant in the competition was only nine years old."
  • Academic competitions: "The contestants in the spelling bee had studied for months."
A Second, Less Common Meaning (Legal Context)

In legal language, a contestant can also refer to a person who formally challenges or disputes a legal document or decision — most commonly, a will (a document that states how a dead person's property should be distributed).

For example: "She was a contestant in the will dispute, arguing that the document had been signed under pressure."

Here, the "competition" is not a game — it is a legal battle. But the core spirit of the word remains the same: this person is actively opposing or contesting something. They are not passively accepting it; they are challenging it.

This legal meaning is rarer in everyday conversation. When most people say "contestant," they mean the competition sense.

Since you're learning, it's worth knowing how this word sits alongside words that feel similar but are not identical:

  • Competitor — Also someone in a competition, but this word puts more emphasis on the drive to beat others. All contestants in a competition are competitors, but "competitor" feels more intense and focused on rivalry. You might say two businesses are competitors — you wouldn't call them contestants.
  • Participant — A broader word. A participant is simply someone who takes part in anything — a meeting, a survey, an event. There doesn't need to be any winning or judging involved. Every contestant is a participant, but not every participant is a contestant.
  • Candidate — Used when someone is being considered for a position, a job, or an award. A candidate applies or is put forward, while a contestant actively competes. In politics, you run as a candidate. On a game show, you are a contestant.
  • Entrant — Very close to contestant. An entrant is someone who has entered a competition. The small difference is that entrant simply signals the act of entering, while contestant implies active, ongoing participation in the contest itself.
The Most Important Things to Remember

1. A contestant is always connected to a contest — no contest, no contestant.
  2. They are an active, voluntary participant — not a bystander.
  3. The competition can be almost anything: a quiz, a race, a pageant, a talent show, or even a legal dispute.
  4. In everyday life, you will encounter this word most often in the context of television competitions, sports, and public events.
